**Ten and Two**

Nobody trusted my grandmother with a car, which was strange, because she'd been driving longer than any of us had been alive. But she was seventy-eight, and her reaction times were theoretical, and my mother had opinions about all of it.

Then I turned fifteen and got my learner's permit, and somebody had to sit in the passenger seat while I practiced, and my father traveled, and my mother worked evenings, and Grandma raised her hand like we were in church.

"That's not happening," my mother said.

So on Tuesdays, when my mother had her shift, Grandma took the keys to the gray Crown Victoria nobody had managed to sell after my grandfather died, and we drove—she drove—the four blocks to the parking lot of St. Anthony's, which emptied out completely after seven o'clock except for one priest who kept his blinds drawn and his business to himself.

The lot became our country. We set up traffic cones borrowed from the church basement to mark intersections. Grandma sat with her purse in her lap like a queen holding a small dog and delivered instruction.

"Both hands on the wheel. Ten and two."

"That's outdated," I said. "Drivers ed says nine and three now."

"They changed it because the airbags will break your arms at ten and two." She waved this off with one ringed hand. "In my day they didn't worry about the airbag breaking your arm. They worried about whether the car had brakes on both sides. Drive."

The first weeks were mostly jerking. Automatic transmissions make it hard to stall, but I found ways to humiliate myself anyway—riding the brake, hopping the curb, killing a cone that never testified. Once, a kid on a bicycle crossed far end of the lot and I panicked and froze with both feet down hard, and the engine made a sound like complaint, and Grandma said, "There. Now you know what your body wants to do when it's scared. Next time it happens, remember that everyone else on the road is scared too, and half of them freeze, so give them room and don't take anything personally."

When I stalled out emotionally—the technical term, according to Grandma—she'd tell stories. How she learned to drive at thirty-six, from a woman named Fran who worked admissions at the same hospital where Grandma filed records, in the parking structure after their shifts, second level, by the ramp.

"My father thought women shouldn't drive. Your grandfather offered to teach me instead, God rest him. He lasted eleven minutes. We came to the intersection of Halsted and Addison, I hesitated on green—" she held up a finger— "*one* hesitation—and he opened the door and got out. Right there in traffic. Walked home. Took him fifty minutes. He always said it was faster than my driving."

"What did he call you after you got your license?" I asked, because I'd heard the nickname somewhere.

"Leadfoot," she said, with unmistakable satisfaction.

One Tuesday in August, I was struggling with backing up, craning over my shoulder, weaving diagonally toward disaster, and Grandma had finally had enough.

"Stop. Watch."

She slid across the bench seat—I remembered later how smoothly she moved, how she didn't brace herself on the dashboard the way she did getting out of chairs—and put it in reverse, one arm over the back of my seat, and backed that boat up forty feet in a perfect curve, straightening the wheel exactly when it needed straightening, ending one precise foot from the fence by the dumpsters.

"How long did you say you hadn't driven?"

"I didn't say," Grandma said.

She looked out the windshield at the fence. The light over the church entrance buzzed on, the way it did at the exact minute the sun went behind the water tower.

"Somebody had to drive your grandfather those last years," she said. "And your uncles worked days. So I took him. Eighteen months of appointments. chemo, the scans, all of it. You get good at anything you do daily. Hospital garages at six in the morning are excellent practice—every level empty, you could back up the entire ramp if you felt like it. Nobody knows that. It's not the kind of thing you mention."

She said it mildly, the way she reported weather. I understood suddenly that everything I knew about her was a rumor.

"Now get out," she said, "and back it up yourself, because I'm tired and I want to go home."

In September I got to drive home for real. Four blocks. Four stops. Grandma sat with her hand hovering near the emergency brake the whole way like a spotter over a weightlifter, coaching quietly—easy roll on the stop sign, watch the lady with the stroller, this light gives you twelve seconds, eleven—and waving me through the four-way with the little flick of her fingers drivers understand instinctively: *go, and I'll deny everything if anything goes wrong.*

We swung into our driveway just as the porch light clicked on and my mother stepped out with her arms already crossed. Grandma rolled down the window.

"She's a natural," she announced.

It wasn't even entirely a lie.

The state required fifty logged practice hours, signed by a licensed driver over twenty-one, and that autumn my mother worked more nights than usual, and somebody's cursive appeared in the signature column—a small, slanted, unnervingly steady hand that wrote *Ruth Kowalczyk* fifty-two times without skipping, next to entries like *parallel parking, residential* and *highway merge (impressive)*.

I passed my road test in October with a score of ninety-eight; lost points for hesitating once on a green, which I consider a tribute.

The Crown Victoria is still in the garage. Every few months the insurance question comes up at dinner, and my mother says it doesn't make sense to keep a car nobody drives, and Grandma butters her bread and says nothing, and looks at me, and I look back at my plate, keeping her secret, and mine, and ours.

message.reasoning:
The user has given me 1000 words and asked me to write whatever comes to me. This is an invitation for creative freedom. Let me think about what would be genuinely interesting or valuable to write with this kind of open prompt.

Options:
1. A short story/fiction piece
2. An essay on something I find interesting
3. Something experimental
4. A meditation on the prompt itself (probably too self-indulgent and meta)

I think fiction is probably the most satisfying response to "write whatever comes to you" — it's a creative writing prompt essentially. Or I could do a personal essay style piece. Let me think about what would actually be interesting.

Fiction idea: Something with emotional resonance, maybe a small quiet story. Quiet stories often work well in short form — a moment of change, an epiphany, something observed. Let me brainstorm:

- A person at a laundromat at 3am
- Someone cleaning out a parent's house after death
- A translator who finds an error in a famous text
- A lighthouse keeper... too clichéd
- Two strangers stuck somewhere
- Someone who works a night job noticing something strange/beautiful
- A child's perspective on adult grief
- Someone learning their grandmother's language

Let me try: cleaning out a house. It's well-trodden but there are fresh angles. Or the laundromat at night — that has good texture potential. Ordinary setting, time to observe, possibility of encounter.

Alternative: an essay. What am I genuinely curious about that would make compelling reading? 

- The history of some mundane object
- Why we dream
- Something about language itself
- Memory and how it works

Actually, let me just write a story. The open prompt "write whatever comes to you" suggests spontaneity, and a story lets me create something whole rather than argue a point. But it should have real craft — not saccharine, not clichéd.

Let me draft a story concept: 

A woman returns to her childhood home while her mother is in hospice/recently died, and discovers something small — letters, a garden, a recording. Hmm.

Or: something less grief-centric since that's very common in AI-generated fiction. What else has genuine feeling?

- A man teaches his daughter to drive. Ordinary but full of texture.
- A piano tuner who hears something odd.
- Someone at an airport during a long delay who decides to abandon their trip.
- A store closing down after decades.
- Someone restoring old photos and finding something.
- The last day of an indoor mall.
- A radio DJ on the last broadcast of a station.
- A woman who writes down her dead father's voicemail before the phone company deletes it.

That last one has something. Voicemails get deleted; people save them by playing them into recordings. Very contemporary grief, very specific technology. But again, grief.

What about joy? Or strangeness? Or beauty without sadness?

Idea: A story about someone who keeps a list. Or about the moment someone changes their life. Or two old friends meeting after decades.

Or magical realism light: every year the town... no, too twee.

How about this: A night-shift worker at a 24-hour diner, and the regulars, and one night something shifts. Diner stories can be great — Melville, Carver territory. Risk: pastiche.

Alternative essay approach: write about writing? No. Write about something like "the ocean as metaphor"? Meh.

Actually here's a thought — maybe I could write something genuinely exploratory: a piece that meditates on time, memory, smallness — but anchored in concrete detail so it doesn't float off into abstraction. Essayistic fiction hybrid, like Annie Dillard or Jenny Offill style. Short paragraphs, fragments, observations accumulating into meaning. That might actually be the most honest answer to "write whatever comes to you" — a mind moving across things.

But readers usually enjoy narrative. Let me commit: a short story with warmth and specificity. Let me pick the driving lesson. Father/daughter or mother/son, parking lot, transmission of knowledge, subtext of growing up and letting go. There's a natural arc in a single lesson: first gear to highway, or just around the lot to the road. Ending: she drives him home, he becomes passenger. That's an earned quiet ending. The subtext writes itself though — risk of predictability. I could gender-swap or complicate: grandmother teaching granddaughter, because everyone else in the family refused. That's fresher — grandma learned to drive late herself, at 40, after divorce or after husband died; teaching is her reclaiming something. Nice.

Or truly different: the person who was hired to close a mall one final time, walking through, turning off lights section by section. Sensory-rich, elegiac, about a whole era. Ends with locking the door. That's atmospheric and I can make it sing.

Between driving-with-grandma and last-night-of-the-mall... The mall piece risks being pure mood without character arc. Grandma driving has an arc, dialogue, humor. Humor matters — the best grief-adjacent pieces leaven with comedy. And "whatever comes to me" invites voice.

Let me sketch: Third person or first? First person, daughter/narrator, named grandma — let's call her nonna? Or just Grandma June. Setting: empty church parking lot on a Tuesday evening, summer. Details: the car is grandpa's old Buick/Crown Victoria that nobody wanted to sell; grandma claims it. Teaching sequence: seat adjustment ("sit up"), mirrors, hands at ten and two vs nine and three (generational dispute over technique — funny). First lurch forward, stalling automatic... no wait, stalling implies manual. Grandma's car would be an automatic. Okay: instead of stalling, she does the classic brake-gas confusion panic moment; narrator calms. Grandma tells stories mid-lesson — about learning to drive at 38 from a man at the grain elevator / from a coworker / secretly. Grandpa never knew she learned? Or grandpa taught her and was terrible at it — screaming passenger. She swore she'd teach differently if ever given the chance. Grandkids line up for license; parents exhausted; grandma volunteers. Nobody trusts her. She's 78. 

Complication for the middle: the actual turn onto the road. Fear. Grandma says something true — small wisdom, not fortune cookie. Maybe: "Everyone out there is scared too. That's why they're all going slow." No—traffic isn't slow. Maybe: "The trick isn't confidence. The trick is not caring if anyone honks." Hmm. Or about how she drove grandpa to chemo for two years and none of the kids knew because she hid the fear. Maybe too heavy? Actually that could be the reveal — the narrator learns grandma has been driving all along to the hospital, that the "we should sell the car" assumption is wrong, that her competence exceeds expectation. Twist: grandma takes the wheel to demonstrate, and suddenly does a perfect reverse park, then reveals: she drove grandpa to all his appointments after his eyesight failed... no wait, he shouldn't drive then; she drove — everyone thought Uncle Rick did. So the "lesson" is theater; she wanted company, or wanted to pass something on deliberately, to give the narrator credit hours. Reason for theater: mom won't let narrator practice with grandma; parents think she's too old; this lot session is their conspiracy. They both keep the secret. The secret binds them. Ending: grandma slides over, narrator drives them home slowly through town, grandma narrating like a flight instructor — easy turns, watch the cyclist — and then a final image: hands, wheel, streetlights coming on. Last line something quiet like "By the time we pulled into the driveway, my mother was on the porch with her arms crossed, but Nonna rolled down the window and said, 'She's a natural,' and it wasn't even entirely a lie."

Good. Warmth + humor + slight poignancy, not maudlin. First person narrator — gender unspecified or lightly female. Name the grandma: Grandma Violet? Ruthie? "My grandmother" plus once: "Grandma Pascarella"? Italian adds flavor. Keep simple: Grandma. Nickname from grandfather: he called her Rocket? Cute: grandpa called her "Leadfoot." Ha — the man who screamed at her driving nicknamed her Leadfoot lovingly. Could work.

Word budget: ~1000 words. They said "you have 1000 words" — treat as target. Aim 950–1000.

Title? Optional. A title is nice: "Right Turn Only," "Empty Lot," "Ten and Two," "Grandma's Parking Lot." "Ten and Two" clean.

Draft mentally:

Opening line strong: "Nobody trusted my grandmother with a car, which was unfair, because she had been driving longer than any of us had been alive."

Then situation: narrator 15 with permit; parents busy/scared; grandma volunteers. Mom vetoes. Tuesdays when mom works late, they take the Crown Victoria to St. Brigid's lot.

Middle beats:
1. Ritual: mirror checks, seat, grandma's rules ("both hands, and don't trust the mirror behind your neck").
2. Technique dispute: ten-and-two vs nine-and-three; grandma scoffs at new methods: "In my day they told us ten and two so airbags could break our arms."
3. First attempts: jerkiness, curb hop? Small comedy: knocking over cone they placed from church supply closet. Narrator panics at bike crossing; grandma calm.
4. Story time: how she learned at 36 from Frank/Zia at the plant; grandpa tried teaching once, lasted eleven minutes, got out of the car at a red light — great comic beat: "He got out at the intersection of Halsted and Addison and walked home. Took him an hour. He said it was faster than my driving."
5. Reveal layering: narrator notices muscle memory — grandma straightens wheel as demonstration; parallel parks perfectly between church dumpsters-ish. Asks. Grandma shrugs: "Four years of hospital runs. Somebody had to drive your grandfather, and your uncles worked days." Chemo reveal.
6. Final stretch: grandma says park it, then "now drive us home before your mother calls." Narrator drives real streets. Grandma narrating gently, hand hovering near emergency brake.
7. Ending on porch, mom arms crossed, grandma: "She's a natural." Understated closer.

Maybe better ending inside car just before driveway — headlights sweeping the driveway, porch light on, grandma's line, and final short sentence: narrator thinking about how everyone in that family learned everything important from somebody pretending to teach. Or end purely on dialogue + image. Aim resonance over explanation: "and it wasn't even entirely a lie" — good wry note; maybe extend one beat: that fall narrator passes test; grandma couldn't come (or comes?), signs the certificate section... Actually: parental signature needed for permit practice log! Real detail: practice-hour logs signed by licensed driver over 21. Detail idea: "Somebody over twenty-one had to sign my hour log, and my mother worked nights that autumn, and somebody's handwriting looked suspiciously steady for a woman of seventy-eight." Lovely closure: the logs grandma signed = documented lie/secrets in ink. End there? Strong. Sequence: porch scene -> log detail as final paragraph.

Careful on facts: US rules vary; typical: permit holder must practice with licensed driver 21+. Log hours (e.g., 50) signed. That reads true broadly; keep generic enough.

Also handle POV age: narrator now older recounting? Simplest: recent-past telling, so reflections minimal, present scene vivid. Fine.

Names: Grandpa Emil? Unneeded name; "my grandfather" fine. Uncles mentioned unnamed. Mom unnamed. Church: St. Adalbert's? Any parish name okay; use generic "St. Brendan's" or non-denominational "the church on Ninth Street" to avoid specificity issues — keep "St. Anthony's" harmless. Crown Victoria gray like dirty nickel.

Humor lines inventory (pick few): 
- "At seventy-eight, her reaction times were theoretical."
- Airbag arms joke.
- Grandfather walking home from red light — centerpiece anecdote, place at low point of lesson to lift morale.
- Cone casualty: "The cone never testified."

Emotional beat placement: demonstration reveal roughly 600-word mark; shift tone momentarily soft: hospital parking garages, gowns' smell, radio low, practicing reversing in empty garage levels at dawn. One restrained sentence cluster. Then back out to drive.

Traffic scenario for final drive: four-way stop correctness impresses grandma: "Wave means go, and it also means I'll deny everything if we hit."

Okay drafting prose now carefully within budget, prioritizing rhythm & concreteness.

(Proceeding to compose final piece in full below.)
